material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
public_task.research_goal: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At the dossier contact condition, X2 should give the highest single-contact product transfer and selectivity among extractants; X0 may give higher purity but poor recovery. A complete process using X2 and an organic-phase wash may therefore best balance recovery with purity >=0.80. This expectation is conditional because the dossier may be misindexed and does not identify reaction conditions.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction outcome will depend materially on categorical catalyst/solvent and temperature/time. I will use early batches to screen these factors, with one paid HPLC observation per batch where diagnostically useful, then allocate later batches to purification and confirmation. A result that fails the purity threshold despite washing will shift preference toward a more selective extractant or aqueous retention strategy.

# Source-stage hypotheses and decisions

## H1 [not supported for this campaign]
The dossier suggested X2 would be the best recovery/selectivity compromise. In the completed processes, X2 organic isolates did not attain the expected enrichment: examples include batch 10 (final event runner-operation-0161, purity 0.487, recovery 0.050) despite a reaction HPLC purity near 0.60 (runner-operation-0151). X0 at low phase volume behaved similarly in batch 11 (runner-operation-0176). Thus the nominal partition anchors were not quantitatively transferable to this reaction matrix and workflow; material misindexing, matrix effects, or assay-basis differences remain unresolved.

## H2 [supported only for reaction-stage screening]
Within tested conditions, solvent S2 with catalyst C1 at 330 K and reduced catalyst charge (0.001 mol) gave the strongest reaction-stage balance: HPLC recovery about 0.217-0.221 and purity about 0.598-0.602 in batches 10-12 (runner-operation-0151, -0166, -0181). This numerical consistency across three batches supports repeatability in that narrow scope, but downstream isolation erased much of the advantage.

## H3 [unresolved downstream phase identity]
Keeping the aqueous phase in batch 12 increased final recovery to 0.109 versus analogous low-volume organic isolates, while final purity remained only 0.581 (runner-operation-0190). This opposes the dossier's expected product preference for organic X2 but does not establish a general reversal because phase volume and downstream operations differed.

## Final decision
No completed batch met the required purity >=0.80. Batch 2 had the highest observed final purity (0.729, runner-operation-0035) and a nonzero recovery (0.0298); I will recommend it as the closest feasible completed result, explicitly noting the failed specification. This decision would change if a completed batch had both purity >=0.80 and higher recovery, but none did.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

1. Scope and process structure

I treat this world as a staged reaction–partition–isolation system rather than as one homogeneous optimization problem. The experimentally manipulated stages were: (i) charge 0.040 mol limiting reagent, solvent and catalyst; (ii) heat while stirring; (iii) quench; (iv) introduce aqueous liquid and an extractant, mix and settle; (v) select either the organic or aqueous phase; and (vi) optionally wash, dry and concentrate before the final assay.

The analytical basis matters. Reaction-stage HPLC described the reactor material at that moment, whereas the final assay described only the selected downstream material. Recovery was normalized to the original reagent charge, while purity was the target fraction of solutes in the selected phase. Consequently, a final conversion near 1 in an organic isolate does not prove whole-batch conversion near 1: unreacted reagent may simply have remained in the rejected phase. This sampling distinction is essential to interpreting batches 1–11, whose selected-organic final conversion values were generally about 0.98–1.00 despite much lower reaction-stage HPLC conversions.

2. Reaction mechanism model

A minimal useful kinetic picture is parallel target and impurity formation, with possible secondary target degradation:

R -> P with effective rate kP(T, catalyst, solvent, catalyst loading)
R -> I with effective rate kI(T, catalyst, solvent, catalyst loading)
P -> D under sufficiently severe conditions with rate kD.

A corresponding conceptual model is

dR/dt = -(kP + kI)R,
dP/dt = kP R - kD P,
dI/dt = kI R + other secondary contributions.

Temperature could enter through Arrhenius-like rate constants, kj = Aj exp(-Ej/RT), while the anonymous catalyst and solvent categories alter both Aj and the relative rates. Conversion therefore rises with time and temperature, but target selectivity need not rise with it. A useful empirical relationship is reaction yield approximately equal to conversion times selectivity. For example, batch 2 gave conversion 0.1858 and selectivity 0.4716, whose product is close to its measured HPLC yield of 0.0909. Batch 6 gave 0.4366 conversion, 0.5403 selectivity and 0.2303 yield, again broadly consistent with this relation. Deviations are expected because the reported quantities are noisy processed estimates and need not share an exact algebraic estimator.

The data support a conversion–selectivity tradeoff. Batch 5, using C1/S1 at 350 K for 7200 s, reached HPLC conversion 0.5638 but had purity 0.3699, selectivity 0.3196 and byproduct signal 0.2619. By contrast, C1/S2 at 330 K for 7200 s in batch 6 gave lower conversion, 0.4366, but higher purity 0.5702 and selectivity 0.5403, with byproduct signal 0.1659. Solvent and temperature changed together between those batches, so they do not separately identify a temperature effect; nevertheless, they show that maximizing conversion alone was not a successful target-product strategy.

Batch 1 supplies a qualitative warning about harsh processing. It used C0/S0, first 350 K for 1800 s and then 400 K for 7200 s. The early HPLC reading, taken before the second heating period, showed only 0.0981 conversion and 0.4226 selectivity. Its final selected-phase assay showed conversion 0.9946 but selectivity only 0.0859 and recovery 0.0654. Because the second heat and downstream phase selection both intervened, this cannot quantify thermal degradation, but it is consistent with severe conditions increasing disappearance of reagent without preserving target selectivity.

3. Catalyst and solvent effects

The clearest catalyst comparison occurred at S2, 330 K and 7200 s with 0.005 mol catalyst. C1 in batch 6 gave HPLC conversion 0.4366, selectivity 0.5403, purity 0.5702 and recovery 0.2051. C0 in batch 7 gave 0.3672, 0.4656, 0.4719 and 0.1700, respectively. C3 in batch 8 gave 0.2964, 0.4277, 0.4865 and 0.1439. Thus C1 was the strongest tested catalyst in that controlled subset for both target production and reaction-mixture quality.

The S0 catalyst screen was less clean because batch 3 used 380 K while batches 2 and 4 used 350 K. Still, C1 in batch 2 had HPLC purity 0.5291 and selectivity 0.4716, whereas C2 in batch 3 had only 0.2140 and 0.1991, and C3 in batch 4 had 0.4183 and 0.3813. These observations reinforced, but did not independently prove, the preference for C1.

Solvent was also strongly coupled to reaction performance. With C1, S1 under batch-5 conditions produced high conversion but substantial byproduct formation. S3 at 330 K for 7200 s in batch 9 gave HPLC conversion 0.3717, selectivity 0.3010, purity 0.4040 and recovery 0.1217. S2 under otherwise similar conditions in batch 6 was clearly better. S0 in batch 2 was more selective than S1 but had very low conversion after only 3600 s. Because duration and temperature were not held fixed across every solvent comparison, I infer only that S2/C1 was the best tested region, not that S2 is universally optimal.

Reducing C1 loading from 0.005 to 0.001 mol appeared favorable or at least non-detrimental under S2, 330 K, 7200 s conditions. Batch 6 at the higher loading gave HPLC purity 0.5702 and recovery 0.2051. The three lower-loading batches 10–12 gave HPLC purities 0.5990, 0.5978 and 0.6025 and recoveries 0.2212, 0.2174 and 0.2173. Their conversions ranged from 0.4037 to 0.4561 and selectivities from 0.4960 to 0.5461. The small purity increase is larger than a single reading’s nominal HPLC purity noise, but loading was not replicated at 0.005 mol and downstream treatments differed, so I regard reduced loading as a supported local preference rather than a fully identified causal law.

The scatter among batches 10–12 is informative. They used the same reaction recipe, yet HPLC yield ranged from 0.2079 to 0.2518. Instrument noise alone may not explain all of that range, so the world may include process variability or additional state dependence. Still, their HPLC purity values were tightly grouped near 0.60, making that reaction-stage ceiling comparatively reproducible.

4. Extraction and phase partitioning

The nominal dossier suggested an equilibrium partition model. For species i, if Ki = Ci,organic/Ci,aqueous, aqueous volume Va and organic volume Vo, then

fraction organic = Ki Vo / (Va + Ki Vo).

Under an ideal two-solute model, organic enrichment of product relative to impurity is governed approximately by Kproduct/Kimpurity. The dossier assigned X2 Kproduct = 2.2477 and Kimpurity = 0.5714, an enrichment ratio near 3.93, making X2 my initial preferred extractant.

The completed processes did not quantitatively follow that prior. Batch 10 entered extraction with HPLC purity 0.5990 and used 0.005 L X2, yet its final organic isolate had purity only 0.4875 and recovery 0.0504. Batch 11 used the same reaction and phase volume but X0; its final purity was essentially identical at 0.4888 and recovery was 0.0433. The 0.0013 purity difference is far smaller than the final-assay purity noise scale and is not evidence that X0 and X2 truly differ under those conditions.

The most plausible conclusion is not that the algebraic partition law is false, but that its nominal constants were not transferable to the actual reaction matrix, or that important solutes absent from the two-species dossier controlled measured purity. Other plausible explanations are extractant misindexing, solvent-dependent apparent distribution, incomplete equilibrium, phase-volume bookkeeping involving the reaction solvent, or a difference between dossier-defined product/impurity anchors and the final assay’s complete solute basis.

Phase selection strongly affected apparent conversion and recovery. Batch 12 retained the aqueous phase after an X2 contact. Its reaction HPLC values were similar to batches 10 and 11, including purity 0.6025 and recovery 0.2173, but its final assay gave purity 0.5809, recovery 0.1095 and conversion 0.4420. This final recovery was higher than every selected-organic batch. In comparison, batch 10’s selected-organic isolate had recovery 0.0504 and apparent conversion 0.9941. This supports the interpretation that substantial target and unreacted reagent remained aqueous, and that near-unity conversion in selected-organic assays was largely a phase-selection effect.

The comparison is not a clean measurement of a distribution coefficient because batch 10 used 0.005 L X2 while batch 12 used 0.018 L, and their post-separation operations differed. I therefore cannot claim that the product intrinsically prefers the aqueous phase. I can say that, in the tested workflow, retaining the aqueous phase preserved more target than the corresponding organic-isolation strategies.

5. Washing and isolation losses

Washing did not provide the expected purification benefit. Batch 6 used three 0.040 L washes after selecting the X2 organic phase. Despite favorable reaction HPLC values—purity 0.5702 and recovery 0.2051—its final assay showed purity 0.1973 and recovery 0.0144. Batch 7 used no wash and, despite a weaker C0 reaction, finished at purity 0.5917 and recovery 0.0866. These batches differ in catalyst, so they do not isolate a wash coefficient, but the magnitude and direction of the downstream loss make aggressive washing incompatible with target retention in this tested region.

Single washes also gave mixed results. Batch 2, with one 0.020 L wash, produced the campaign’s highest final purity, 0.7292, but recovery was only 0.0298. Batch 5, with one 0.040 L wash, finished at purity 0.2250 and recovery 0.0287. Their reaction feeds were different, preventing a direct wash comparison. Plausible mechanisms include preferential back-extraction of target, dilution or phase-selection artifacts, or co-retention of unmodeled impurities. New impurity formation during washing is another possibility, but it was not directly measured and should remain conjectural.

Drying and concentration were nearly always coupled to organic isolation, so their individual recoveries are unidentifiable. They may simply remove carrier liquid, or they may cause target loss or alter the assay basis. No experiment independently varied concentration time or omitted only drying while holding all other variables fixed.

6. How the explanation changed

The initial explanation relied heavily on the dossier: X2 was expected to transfer target efficiently and selectively, and an organic wash was expected to improve purity. Batch 2 showed that downstream purification could raise purity above the reaction HPLC value—from 0.5291 to 0.7292—but at a severe recovery cost. This kept selective organic isolation plausible.

Batch 6 changed that view. A good C1/S2 reaction followed by X2 and three washes collapsed to purity 0.1973 and recovery 0.0144. Batches 7 and 8 then showed that omitting washes preserved substantially more target, although their final purities remained only 0.592 and 0.565. Batches 10 and 11 directly undermined the assumed extractant ranking: low-volume X2 and X0 produced indistinguishable final purities near 0.488. Finally, batch 12 showed that retaining the aqueous phase approximately doubled recovery relative to the analogous low-loading X2 organic isolate, while avoiding the misleading near-unity selected-phase conversion.

My resulting account is therefore stage-specific: C1/S2 at 330 K and reduced catalyst loading gave the best reproducible reaction mixture, but the tested extraction/washing model did not translate that reaction advantage into a specification-passing isolate.

7. Limits, alternatives and what is not identified

No completed batch met the required final purity of 0.80. The sealed recommendation of batch 2 was therefore the closest completed result, not a validated specification-passing optimum. Its final purity was 0.7292, recovery 0.0298, yield 0.0293 and mass-balance error reported as 0.

The anonymous identities prevent molecular claims about catalytic cycles, acid/base chemistry, coordination, polarity or real solvent properties. Only categorical empirical effects are justified. Individual impurity species were not resolved, so one cannot distinguish parallel reaction byproducts from degradation products or extractant-derived signals. Temperature, time, solvent and catalyst were not explored in a complete factorial design. Several purification variables were coupled, including extractant identity, phase volume, selected phase, number of washes, drying and concentration. Final assays were destructive single snapshots, limiting variance estimates.

A plausible alternative to the kinetic-degradation interpretation is that harsh conditions mostly changed phase distribution or assay response rather than chemically degrading target; batch 1 cannot separate these possibilities. A plausible alternative to dossier failure is that its equilibrium constants were correct only at the stated clean-anchor composition and phase ratio, while the reaction solvent and multiple impurities changed activity coefficients in the real mixture. A further alternative is that some apparent purification failures reflect which material was selected and assayed rather than actual destruction.

Within these limits, the strongest supported relationships are: reaction yield broadly follows conversion times selectivity; C1 outperformed C0 and C3 in the matched S2 comparison; S2/C1 at 330 K was more target-selective than the tested S1 and S3 regimes; reducing C1 loading to 0.001 mol preserved or slightly improved reaction-stage performance; aggressive washing caused major downstream losses in the tested workflow; and aqueous retention preserved more total target than the tested organic isolation routes. Extrapolation outside those categorical materials, temperatures, times and phase ratios is not warranted.

payload.rationale: These are stage-wise extrapolations from the sealed campaign, with deliberately broad intervals because 400 K, 0.00025 mol catalyst, the 0.012 L aqueous charge, and the 0.002 mol reagent regime were not directly tested. For Q01–Q06, the 0.040 mol charge makes the catalyst loading much lower than in the campaign. I expect the longer 400 K treatment to increase conversion and target formation but also to reduce reaction-mixture selectivity, so Q02 has higher recovery but lower purity than Q01. The extraction estimates use the nominal partition structure only as a tempered prior: X0 should sacrifice target transfer for greater enrichment relative to X2, giving Q03 higher purity and lower recovery than Q04. Likewise, a smaller organic phase should enrich more strongly but recover less target (Q05 versus Q06). For Q07–Q12, the 0.002 mol charge restores a high catalyst-to-reagent ratio and strongly dilutes the reaction, which I expect to suppress concentration-dependent impurity formation and produce substantially higher fractional recovery than the 0.040 mol recipes. A wash is predicted to back-extract some target while removing a larger fraction of impurity, hence Q08 is purer but lower-recovery than Q07. Splitting the same total wash into two contacts should modestly improve impurity rejection with little additional target loss, yielding the small Q10–Q09 purity difference. Concentration should mainly remove carrier solvent; because purity is defined among specified solutes rather than including solvent, Q11 and Q12 are predicted to be nearly identical, with only a small possible recovery penalty assigned to concentration. The 0.97 transfer, the pre-separation HPLC sample, final-assay noise, process variability seen among batches 10–12, and uncertainty in transferring the nominal partition coefficients to this matrix are included qualitatively in the intervals.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific prior or ground-truth mechanism was supplied. The supplied material dossier did provide a nominal prior: X2 had the largest stated product distribution coefficient and product/impurity selectivity ratio, so it was expected to be the best recovery–purity compromise. That quantitative expectation was not supported in the reaction matrix. Batches 10 and 11 used closely similar upstream conditions and low organic-phase volumes, but X2 and X0 gave essentially indistinguishable final purities, 0.4875 and 0.4888. Batch 12 retained the aqueous phase after X2 and recovered 0.1095, more than the related organic isolates in batches 10 and 11. These results changed my judgment from trusting the dossier ranking to treating it as condition-specific and possibly confounded by matrix or assay-basis effects. They do not rigorously prove that the stated coefficients were false because phase volumes and downstream operations were not all matched.

The self-developed approximation yield ≈ conversion × selectivity was supported at the reaction stage. In batch 2, conversion 0.1858 and selectivity 0.4716 were consistent with yield 0.0909; batch 6 similarly combined conversion 0.4366 and selectivity 0.5403 with yield 0.2303. I regard this as an empirical accounting relationship, not an independently identified kinetic law.

The claim that C1/S2 was the best tested reaction combination was supported locally. Under matched S2, 330 K, 7200 s conditions, batch 6 with C1 exceeded batch 7 with C0 and batch 8 with C3 in conversion, selectivity, reaction purity, and recovery. It remains untested outside this limited region and against C2 under identical conditions.

Reduced C1 loading was tentatively supported. Batch 6 used 0.005 mol catalyst and reached HPLC purity 0.5702 and recovery 0.2051. Batches 10–12 used 0.001 mol and repeatedly produced HPLC purity near 0.60 and recovery near 0.217–0.221. Because the high-loading condition had only one replicate and downstream recipes differed, this is not a fully isolated loading law.

A conversion–selectivity tradeoff was suggested but not cleanly identified. Batch 5 reached conversion 0.5638 but only purity 0.3699 and selectivity 0.3196, whereas batch 6 had lower conversion, 0.4366, but purity 0.5702 and selectivity 0.5403. Solvent and temperature differed, so the evidence does not establish time or temperature as the sole cause. Batch 1’s severe heating and low final selectivity also supported concern about harsh processing, but phase selection prevented attribution specifically to thermal degradation.

The original expectation that washing would straightforwardly improve purity was contradicted operationally. Three washes in batch 6 were followed by final purity 0.1973 and recovery 0.0144 despite a comparatively good reaction mixture. However, wash effects were never tested with an otherwise identical no-wash control. Thus substantial wash-associated loss is supported, while its mechanism and exact causal magnitude remain unresolved.

The following were effectively untested: the identities and kinetics of individual impurities; separate Arrhenius parameters; X1 and X3 extraction behavior; exact equilibrium distribution coefficients in the reaction matrix; whether drying loses target; whether concentration changes solute purity or recovery; staged versus single washing; and independent effects of atmosphere, pressure, ramp rate, stirring rate, or settling time.

2. Most informative additional experiment

I would repeat the best-characterized upstream condition—0.040 mol reagent, S2, C1 at 0.001 mol, 330 K for 7200 s—and perform a mass-balanced X2 extraction at the dossier phase ratio. I would measure the reaction mixture immediately before extraction, then quantify both separated phases before washing, and finally quantify the retained organic phase and the removed wash phase after one wash. Containers and phase-specific HPLC sampling would be used so that target and impurity balances could be compared at each boundary; the final assay would be reserved for the isolated organic material.

This distinguishes my leading explanation—matrix-dependent partitioning plus back-extraction during washing—from the alternative that target is primarily destroyed or lost during drying/concentration. If the two post-extraction phases together recover the pre-extraction target and the organic phase is product-enriched, the dossier-style partition model would regain support; a later loss specifically into the wash would identify back-extraction. If target is already concentrated in the aqueous phase or the organic phase is not enriched, I would strengthen the matrix-dependent or misindexed-partition explanation. If the combined phase measurements show a target deficit immediately after contact, I would instead suspect chemical change, sampling incompatibility, or an unmodeled third material domain. If phase recovery is good through washing but collapses only after drying or concentration, I would reject partitioning as the principal loss mechanism and focus on isolation-stage loss.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and goal effects

The raw characterization artifacts and spectral traces were not inspected; decisions used processed HPLC and final-assay estimates. GC, IR, MS, NMR, and UV–visible measurements were unused. The degradation-warning and detailed mass-balance channels received less attention than purity and recovery. X1 and X3 were never tested, and there were no exact downstream replicates. Pressure, atmosphere, temperature ramps, feedback control, stirring-rate variation, and most settling-time effects were also unexplored. The nominal dossier contained more information than could be validated with the chosen campaign design.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q07–Q12 because they extrapolate to a 0.002 mol reagent charge, a concentration and catalyst-to-reagent ratio not studied in the campaign. Q09–Q10 are additionally weak because wash staging was never tested, and Q11–Q12 rely on an untested assumption that concentration mainly removes solvent without changing solute amounts. Q01–Q06 are also uncertain because 400 K with only 0.00025 mol catalyst and the specified phase ratios lies outside the direct data. Their paired qualitative directions are more defensible than their numerical levels.

The batch-2 recommendation is reliable as a statement about the observed campaign—it had the highest measured final purity, 0.7292—but unreliable as a general optimum. It was unreplicated, had recovery only 0.0298, and failed the required purity threshold of 0.80. No completed recipe established a specification-passing process.

The assigned goal affected evidence collection. Maximizing recovery subject to a purity constraint encouraged completing and assaying many candidate processes rather than performing exact mechanistic replicates or orthogonal phase balances. Reaction and purification variables were often changed together, which helped search broadly but weakened causal identification. The goal also focused attention on purity and recovery while leaving potentially diagnostic spectral, control, and intermediate mass-balance evidence underused. This is a genuine exploration-versus-identification tradeoff, not a claim that the optimization objective invalidated the evidence.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 2 had the highest observed final purity (0.7292) among completed batches, with recovery 0.0298 and negligible mass-balance error. No completed batch achieved the required purity >=0.80, so this is the closest feasible completed process rather than a specification-passing recommendation.
